title: Magnetism and Electromagnetism
seo_title: Year 11 Science: Magnetism and Electromagnetism Worksheets (GCSE Combined Science)
standard_text: Poles of a magnet; permanent and induced magnetism and magnetic forces; magnetic fields and the Earth's field; the magnetic effect of a current; solenoids and electromagnets; (higher tier) Fleming's left-hand rule, the motor effect (F = BIl) and electric motors.
meta_desc: Free Year 11 GCSE Combined Science worksheets on magnetism: poles, magnetic materials, field lines, electromagnets, the motor effect, F = BIl and Fleming's left-hand rule. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Like poles repel; unlike poles attract.
key_sub: Force on a wire = flux density × current × length (F = BIl).
body_html:
How to think about it

Currents make magnetic fields, and magnetic fields push on currents.

  • Field lines go from north to south. Iron, steel, nickel and cobalt are magnetic.
  • An electromagnet is stronger with more turns, a larger current and an iron core.
  • F = BIl. Fleming's left-hand rule: first finger field, second finger current, thumb motion.
Example

B = 0.5 T, I = 2 A, l = 0.1 m. Force?

0.5 × 2 × 0.1

Answer: 0.1 N

Example

North near south?

Unlike poles

Answer: attract

Common mistakes

  • Thinking all metals are magnetic.
  • Drawing field lines from south to north.
  • Mixing up the fingers in Fleming's left-hand rule.

faq.q: How can you make an electromagnet stronger?
faq.a: Use more turns of wire, a larger current, or put an iron core inside the coil.
A wire carrying a current in a magnetic field feels a force. The force F = BIl when the wire is at right angles to the field.

faq.q: How do you use Fleming's left-hand rule?
faq.a: Point your first finger along the field (north to south), your second finger along the current, and your thumb shows the direction of the force.

items.q: How does a electric motor work?

A changing current in one coil induces a current in another coil.
items.e: Electricity and magnetism are linked.
